## Slide 01 — Grading Is Easy, Feedback Is Hard · 00:00 - 00:30

> Delivery: Say the title, then move on. Do not read the author list aloud.

Good morning. Our paper is called Grading Is Easy, Feedback Is Hard, and the
artifact I want to show you is the machinery behind that title.

It is a replication package for evaluating large language models as instructor-
support tools on a design-oriented object-oriented programming assignment.
Eighty-four real Java submissions, two models, a complete prompt protocol, and
every intermediate file.

Everything I show runs on your laptop without an API key.

---

## Slide 02 — Why This Artifact Exists · 00:30 - 01:15

First, why we needed an artifact at all.

In our OOP course students refactor a deliberately weak codebase, so
correctness and design pull apart. Submission A can pass every feature check
while being one four-hundred-line class with no domain objects. Submission B
can have a single off-by-one bug on top of a clean class model.

Unit tests and static analysis rank A above B. An instructor does not.

So this assessment stays manual: eighty-four submissions, seven rubric criteria
each, plus written feedback, across twenty-eight teaching assistants.

The obvious question is whether an LLM can help. The harder one is how you
would measure "help" at all.

---

## Slide 03 — What Is Inside The Artifact · 01:15 - 01:50

Here is what you get.

src/prompt is the grading protocol - eight files, and I would argue that is the
real contribution. src/pipeline and src/workflows are twenty-three scripts:
render prompts, call providers, validate outputs, compute statistics. And
reproduce.py rebuilds the entire paper in one command.

Then the data: six run directories, two models times three repetitions. Each
holds the anonymized submissions, the rubric, one thousand and eight rendered
prompts - the exact bytes we sent - five hundred and four model assessments,
the TA grades and the expert reference.

---

## Slide 04 — The Prompt (1/3): Two Stages, On Purpose · 01:50 - 02:55

Now the prompt, because that is what people usually want to see. We split
grading into two calls, deliberately.

Stage one is scoring only - the prompt forbids student-facing prose here. For
every rubric criterion the model must return a score, positive evidence of
learning, observations that should not cost points, and a list of deductions.
Every deduction is structured: points lost, severity, confidence, which rubric
requirement it anchors to, the problem, the consequence, how to fix it, and
references into the code. Plus a reviewer-audit block flagging what a human
should double-check.

Only then does stage two turn that validated JSON into feedback. It is told not
to re-grade and not to look for new defects. It selects at most six high-
confidence items and writes them for a first-year student.

The split makes the two failure modes separable: when a grade is wrong, you can
point at the deduction that caused it.

---

## Slide 05 — The Prompt (2/3): Dynamic Injection · 02:55 - 03:55

This is the part I would actually reuse, so let me be concrete. Nothing in that
prompt directory is a finished prompt - they are templates with double-brace
placeholders, filled at two distinct moments.

At build time, the render script resolves nine slots for stage one: the
specification, the grading reference, the starter scaffold, and the rubric -
which is gated, so the script refuses to render if the rubric is not marked
ready. Plus the course principles, the calibration examples and the schema. A
hundred and thirty-six lines of template become a seventeen-hundred-line
prompt.

Stage two is the interesting one. One placeholder is deliberately left
unresolved on disk; at call time the runner parses the stage one response, re-
serializes it, and only then injects it.

Two consequences. Stage two never sees raw model prose, only validated JSON.
And since that substitution is the only non-static step, the prompts we ship
are a faithful audit trail.

---

## Slide 06 — The Prompt (3/3): The Guardrails · 03:55 - 04:45

The templates are only half of it. The other half is the guardrails, and every
one of them exists because the model got something wrong without it.

We had to write, literally: do not convert optional improvements into point
loss - route them to a separate non-penalized observations list. Avoid double
jeopardy: if one root cause produces five symptoms, deduct once, on the
criterion it most affects. Do not penalize naming, formatting, casing or
punctuation. Here is the severity scale in actual points, because moderate
means nothing on its own. And if confidence is low, keep it out of the
student's feedback and log the omission for the reviewer.

The two JSON schemas are hard contracts, and the pipeline validates every
single response against them.

---

## Slide 07 — How The Study Was Run · 04:45 - 05:30

How the study was actually run, in three phases.

Phase one, inputs. Submissions are anonymized: author lines masked, repository
names replaced, identifiers reduced to S01 through S84. No raw student
repositories and no identity mapping ship in the artifact.

Phase two, evaluation. Three sources of judgement: the TA grades, which are the
authentic operational baseline; an expert reference, meaning rubric scores plus
three hundred sixty-one annotated issues over a twelve-category taxonomy; and
the LLM assessments - both models, three runs each, five hundred and four
assessments.

Phase three, the analyses for our two research questions, plus run-to-run
stability.

The detail I would highlight for reuse: every run directory is self-contained.

---

## Slide 08 — The Hard Measurement: Is It The Same Problem? · 05:30 - 06:10

One measurement was genuinely hard.

To ask whether the model found the same problem as the expert, string equality
is useless and taxonomy overlap is far too generous. Two evaluators describe
one encapsulation defect in completely different words.

So we used a third model, Claude Sonnet 5, as adjudicator - from a provider
family we were not evaluating, so neither model gets a home advantage. Matching
is scoped to one submission and one criterion.

That is model-assisted labelling, so we call it operational matching, not
ground truth. The prompt, the model identifier and every cache entry ship in
the artifact.

> Optional, only if ahead of the clock: "and there is a sensitivity check -
> reversing ten adjudicated matches shifts precision and recall by under four
> hundredths."

---

## Slide 09 — What The Numbers Say · 06:10 - 07:00

The results, briefly.

On grades, Gemini essentially matches the human baseline: mean absolute error
of 0.44 against the expert reference, where the TAs themselves sit at 0.45.
GPT-5.5 systematically undergrades, with a bias of minus 1.45.

On diagnosis, the F1 scores are almost identical - 0.67 and 0.65 - and that
similarity hides completely opposite behaviour. GPT-5.5 finds nearly every
expert-annotated issue, recall 0.96, but about half of what it reports has no
expert equivalent. Gemini is much cleaner and misses over a third of the
issues.

And stability: both models rank submissions consistently, ICC around 0.9, yet
exact agreement across three runs is two percent and zero.

Same aggregate F1, a different assessment instrument. That is the title.

---

## Slide 10 — Reproduce It · 07:00 - 07:45

So, reproducing it. Three commands: virtual environment, install requirements,
run reproduce.

No API keys, no Docker, no GPU. I re-checked on a clean Ubuntu machine while
preparing this talk: thirteen seconds end to end, and every markdown table came
back byte-identical to the paper.

There are flags for the triangulation analyses, and one to re-run the models
themselves - and we warn you there, because provider models drift, so those
numbers may not match ours.

To reuse it for your own course: replace the rubric and the specification, drop
your submissions in, and keep the prompt directory. That is the transferable
part.

---

## Slide 11 — Takeaway · 07:45 - 08:00

To close: we are not shipping a grader. We are shipping a way to measure one -
separately for grade calibration and for diagnostic coverage, on authentic
submissions, in one command.

Thank you - happy to take questions.

## If you are running long

Cut in this order. Each cut is self-contained and costs no continuity.

1. **Slide 02, the A/B example** (~20 s). Replace with: "correctness and design
   do not agree in this assignment, so grading stays manual."
2. **Slide 06, the severity scale and the low-confidence rule** (~15 s). Keep
   double jeopardy and the optional-improvements rule; those land best.
3. **Slide 07, phase one** (~15 s). The anonymization detail moves to Q&A.
4. **Slide 03, the byte counts** (~10 s). The directory tree is on the slide
   anyway.

Do not cut slides 04, 05 or 10. The prompt structure, the injection mechanism and the one-command reproduction are what the audience came for.

## If you are running short

Expand slide 06 with a concrete miss: GPT-5.5 kept reporting Javadoc phrasing
and naming inherited from the starter code as penalizable deductions, even
though the prompt routes optional improvements elsewhere. That is exactly why
the guardrail text ships in the artifact and not just in the paper.

Slide 05 has room for the failure mode the gate prevents: an unfinished rubric
silently rendering into 84 prompts. `ensure_rubric_ready` turns that into a
hard stop before a single API call is made.

Slide 09 also has room for submission S02: the expert deducted 3.5 points for
an off-by-one error on array access, Gemini caught it, and GPT-5.5 missed it
despite its higher aggregate recall. Aggregate profiles are tendencies, not
guarantees.

## Question prep

**Isn't using an LLM to judge LLM output circular?**
Partly, and we label it as operational matching rather than ground truth. Three
mitigations: the adjudicator comes from a third provider family, so it is not
grading its own vendor; matching is scoped to one submission and one criterion
at a time rather than free-form; and we ship the prompt, the model identifier
and every cache entry so you can audit or replace it. Independent human
validation is future work.

**Why only one expert annotator?**
It is a stated threat to validity. The reference is structured validity
evidence for one consistent rubric application, not consensus ground truth.
Multi-rater references are explicitly future work.

**Why three runs?**
Three runs characterize output variability under a fixed protocol without
estimating the full distribution - enough to show that exact agreement across
runs is near zero, which was the finding we needed. We flag the limitation.

**Why inject the Stage 1 JSON at run time instead of rendering it in?**
Because Stage 1 output does not exist until Stage 1 has run, and it changes on
every repetition. Rendering it in would make the prompt files run-specific.
Leaving one placeholder open means the shipped prompts stay diffable across the
six runs, and the only varying input is the JSON we also ship under outputs/.

**Does the model ever see its own raw Stage 1 text?**
No. The runner parses the response and re-serializes it before substitution, so
Stage 2 receives normalized JSON. If Stage 1 emits something unparseable, the
run fails there rather than feeding prose into the feedback stage.

**Can I get the raw student repositories?**
No. The anonymized Java sources are included because they are prompt inputs,
but raw repositories, the identity mapping, API keys and raw API traces are not
in the package. Everything reported in the paper still replicates without them.

**Will `--with-apis` give me your numbers?**
Almost certainly not, and the script warns you. Commercial models change on the
provider side. The offline path is the verification path; the API path exists
so you can run the protocol on new models or your own data.

**Which model should I use for my course?**
That is the wrong question, and it is the argument of the paper. Decide the
workflow role first. If you want to audit grades, you want calibration. If you
want candidate issues for an instructor to filter, you want recall. Then pick.

**What did the runs cost, and how long did they take?**
We did not record cost or wall-clock time in the artifact, so I would rather
not guess. Runs two and three used the providers' batch APIs; the config in
each run directory has the request-rate settings we used.
